data.name: Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire
data.detailed_description:
Obsidian Edition



The Obsidian Edition Includes:
• Game Download
• BEAST OF WINTER (Jul 2018): An ancient feud between eldritch powers goes unresolved in the southern seas, and only you can halt the mounting destruction. (post-launch content, a $10 value)
• SEEKER, SLAYER, SURVIVOR (Sep 2018): Far from the bustling trade lanes of the Deadfire Archipelego, the most ambitious warriors of Eora gather to compete for divine favor. (post-launch content, a $10 value)
• THE FORGOTTEN SANCTUM (Nov 2018): The great wizards of Eora have gathered together for a common cause and reach out to you, the Watcher, for assistance. (post-launch content, a $10 value)
• Original Soundtrack: The soundtrack to Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire by Justin Bell, featuring all-new tracks inspired by the peoples and factions of the Deadfire Archipelago.
• Defiant Apparel: This stylish tricorn hat comes with a built-in eyepatch that protects the wearer from a variety of ocular incursions, as well as looking extremely piratical.
• Cosmo, the Space Pig: It wouldn't be Pillars of Eternity without Cosmo! Cosmo accompanies your party, floating on cyan gossamer, inspiring you through a combination of unflappable courage and incredible cuteness.
• Digital P&P Guide: Pillars of Eternity has a strong tradition of adapting and adopting pen-and-paper techniques in our systems and adventure designs. Our designers decided to take that knowledge and give something back to the tabletop community! This pen-and-paper adventuring system has been developed from the ground up by Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire lead designer Josh Sawyer and other members of the Deadfire design team. Connect with other Deadfire fans and create your own adventures!
• Hi-Res Digital Map: This handsome sea chart is suitable for use as a desktop wallpaper or can be printed to assist you with navigating the treacherous waters of the Deadfire Archipelago.
• Digital Guidebook, Vol. II: Created by our friends at Dark Horse Comics, this is the next volume in the comprehensive guide to the world of Pillars of Eternity, filled with the legends, lore, and lost locations of the Deadfire Archipelago. Useful as an adventuring companion, or just to browse and learn more about the intricacies of this deep and enigmatic corner of Eora, the digital guidebook features beautiful illustrations and plenty of fascinating background.


Acerca do jogo


Pursue a rogue god over land and sea in the sequel to the multi-award-winning RPG Pillars of Eternity. Captain your ship on a dangerous voyage of discovery across the vast unexplored archipelago region of the Deadfire. Bend the world to your will, as you explore the depths of infinite possibilities, including detailed character customization, total freedom of exploration, and more meaningful choices at every turn.

• Immerse yourself in a deeper single player RPG game experience - enriched with cutting edge technology and features, Deadfire builds on the foundation of classic D&D gameplay with vastly improved graphics, deeper game mechanics and a whole new hand-crafted adventure where choices truly matter.

• Discover the new region of the Deadfire – plot your own course by ship and explore the rich and exotic islands of the archipelago region, discovering new places interacting with their inhabitants and engaging in a variety of quests at every port.

• Build your party and customize your companions – choose from 7 different companions to join you on your quest and assign multiple classes and deeper abilities for each. Witness their personal relationships and interactions unfold with the addition of the new companion system.


• Captain your ship across the seas – as your stronghold on the seas, your ship is much more than simply a vessel for exploring. Upgrade your ship and crew and choose what skills you improve in order to survive dangerous encounters along the way.

reviews.review:
[b]Short verdict[/b]: a solid CRPG with a somewhat wasted potential due to spreading too thin.

[b]Pillars of Eternity: Deadfire[/b] is a worthy successor to the first game, which was an attempt to bring the classic top-down CRPG experience to modern audiences.
It’s a considerable improvement in its visual presentation, gameplay mechanics, and overall enjoyment. Yet the overall experience is lacking because the game fails to bring all its elements into a cohesive and fun grand adventure, which is probably why [b]Deadfire[/b] initially failed to gain as much popularity as its predecessor.It also seems to have tried to appeal to too many types of players at once.

[list]
[*][b]Companions and the reputation system[/b]: There are 13 companions in total — more than in the first game. On paper, that’s an improvement. However, six of the [b]Deadfire[/b] companions are sidekicks, meaning they have no companion quests or reputation system and significantly fewer random reaction dialogues. For example, sidekick Mirke, who was supposed to be a fully fledged companion, has only a few dialogue lines in the faction quest that leads to recruiting her. After that, she’s just like any other premade adventurer you can hire in a tavern.
Additionally, 4 of the 7 full companions represent the major factions, and, therefore, 3 of them can become hostile to each other for political reasons. This leads to the next point: the reputation system.

There is a reputation system for factions and companions. Companions have personality traits and react to NPCs, the player’s choices, and each other. If you want to maintain positive relationships, this limits your party composition — who you can bring along together on certain quests. That’s where sidekicks come in handy: they don’t trigger reactions and can fill missing roles.
On the other hand, internal discord has no real consequences. The worst that happens is a dialogue where you ask them to get along. Some players might even enjoy the hostile banter. But if it ultimately doesn’t matter, and the relationship system is just for flavour — with, in some cases, barely existing romance paths — what was the point of including it?
I guess the reputation system was implemented to fit a very specific idea of what a classic roleplaying game should be like and how its mechanics should facilitate that. This approach was present in the classic CRPGs that inspired [b]Deadfire[/b], and it’s what the core fans wanted.

Personally, I didn’t enjoy the limitations it imposed or the micromanagement that came with a roster of 13 companions. I would have enjoyed it more if the personality traits weren’t fixed and companions’ beliefs could change.
Otherwise, I’d much rather have had a smaller roster of companions (e.g., 4–6) if that meant longer questlines for each companion and more time spent on the story overall.
I think what I’m trying to say is that the reputation and relationship system was never fully realised. I’d rather have seen that time go toward other aspects of the game.

[*][b]Lore[/b]: Picking up where [b]POE1[/b] left off, [b]Deadfire[/b] has some pretty interesting lore built around the idea that [spoiler]the gods were made by an ancient civilization by combining the souls of certain groups of people to bring order to the natural cycle of reincarnation. As a result, the gods are as imperfect as [strike]humans[/strike] kith, and many current and historical disasters are the result of their [strike]human-like[/strike] kith-like decisions[/spoiler]. There’s more to it, but that’s the simple version. It’s a pretty cool concept.
Unfortunately, there are many logical errors and inconsistencies in the gods’ reasoning and actions. They don’t represent all aspects of the world and society, as a full pantheon should, and they don’t learn from their mistakes — not as beings with their power, perspective, and lifespans should. I can accept the idea of an imperfect divine being, but I cannot accept a divine being incapable of transcending its own prejudices and fallacies despite the otherworldly knowledge and insights it has gathered over millennia. The pantheon exists in the game only as a backdrop for the player’s actions. But it simply was not fully thought through.

[*][b]Quests and story[/b]: The game has a pretty solid, albeit short, main storyline and interesting faction quests. There are also a few decent side quests, but the rest of the game is filler content. The quests are interesting stories in their own right, but at several points, the player is bombarded with new quests. This can be overwhelming on a first playthrough, especially because it tends to happen before you’ve established who’s who and what’s what in each location.

It doesn’t help that some quests take you all around the archipelago. You can miss content or lock yourself into an undesirable outcome if you don’t complete certain quests in a specific order, and the game gives you no hints about that order. All of this results in convoluted, fragmented, and confusing quest progression for first-time players.

Worst of all, some quests are better left unfinished if you care about certain NPCs and endgame outcomes.

[*][b]Factions and Moral Choices[/b]: As mentioned before, I feel that the reputation system reflects a particular idea of how CRPGs should be played. I’d describe this idea as giving players room to roleplay their characters and fill in the gaps with their own imaginations—for example, by asking, “What would my character do in this situation?” The intention is to approximate realism rather than provide perfect outcomes. In my opinion, though, it’s a poor approximation. On the one hand, it offers some room for variability; on the other, it limits player choices to fixed, stereotypical paths. I felt this same approach was reflected in the design and possible outcomes of the faction choices.

There is some moral justification for each of the four main factions, and arguably, all of them are portrayed as equally morally gray, albeit some in more obvious ways than others. The endgame states are vague enough to leave plenty of room for headcanon. To me, all of this makes the choices equally meaningless. I also didn’t enjoy that it wasn’t possible to find a middle ground between the factions. It was all or nothing, which didn’t seem realistic or logical to me.

Ultimately, I chose the Vailians because they stand for scientific progress in the most obvious way, although the vague endgame states mean that this isn’t exclusive to them.

Here’s a simple breakdown of what choosing each faction basically means:

- [u]Vailians[/u]: The scientifically and socially progressive (but greedy and corporate) faction. They’re willing to exploit the natives or work with slavers for profit.
- [u]Rauatai[/u]: An expansionist, militaristic faction that wants to turn the Deadfire Archipelago into a network of fortified kibbutzim and find a way to pacify the storms ravaging its homeland. Its members aren’t above assassination or sabotage, and they believe they have a historical right to settle the Archipelago, where their ancestors lived thousands of years ago.
- [u]Huana[/u]: The underdog natives, with power over water and weather. They may seem like “noble savages” at first, but beneath the surface lies a rotten social hierarchy and a dark past. They’re a good choice if you’re up for a homeland-reclamation story, but a questionable one if you consider the global implications of the main endgame state.
- [u]Principi[/u]: The pirates and, in a way, the Archipelago’s other native population. They began as Old Vailian expatriates and now hope to establish a new homeland shaped by their rebellious, adventurous, freedom-loving culture that doesn't support slavery (unlike Vailians), indentured servitude (unlike Rauatai) or caste system (unlike Huana). Unless you side with Aeldys, in which case, it’s anarchy and full punk mode.

[*][b]World building and exploration[/b]: cont. in the comments
